text.p: Bangladesh went on disaster alert and evacuated half a million people on Monday as a cyclone rampaged from the Bay of Bengal towards the country's flat coastal region, officials said.
Strong winds and tidal waves ripped through the towns of Cox's Bazar and Teknaf, and authorities warned that the core of the cyclone was expected to hit the mainland within two hours.
They fear high seas will inundate much of the vulnerable low-lying Asian nation at a critical harvest time, threatening vital rice crops.
Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina cancelled a planned trip to Spain on Sunday night as the government put the army and navy on high alert for emergency rescue and relief operations.
Bangladesh's worst cyclone in 1991 killed at least 138,000 people and left millions homeless.

"It's definite the high velocity cyclone will hit us soon," said Ali Imam Majumder, the deputy commissioner of Cox's Bazar. "The maximum windspeed will be 200 kmh (112 mph) or more. Vast coastal areas may be inundated by a five metre (15 foot) sea surge," he told Reuters.
Over 33,000 Red Crescent and other volunteers have evacuated about half a million people to cyclone shelters, officials said.
Over 130,000 people were moved to shelters in Cox's Bazar district alone, Majumder said.
Air force planes from Chittagong base were moved to Dhaka while the navy sent its vessels to safety.
Fishermen have been warned not to leave port and coastal officials had been told to hoist "great danger" signals.
Dozens of ships berthed at Chittagong and Mongla ports were moved to outer anchorages, port officials said.
"We are taking this precaution so the ships do not collide during the storm and jam the channel by sinking," said Chittagong Port Harbourmaster Quamrul Islam.
State-run radio and television broadcast frequent storm warnings.
People fleeing their homes or being moved to cyclone shelters have been asked to store drinking water, food and other essentials underground to help them after the cyclone.
A ministerial meeting in Dhaka on Sunday said attempts would be made to minimise economic losses.
"We can't do anything about the damage done (by cyclone) but will effort to contain losses in the aftermath," one official said without giving details.
Bangladesh is currently harvesting Boro, one of the main rice varieties cultivated in the country, which can be affected by strong winds, officials said.
"It's too early to predict anything but let's hope for the best," one official said on Monday.
